stories.title: Engagement with independent group to resume on pay row
stories.summary: Trade unions and Government representatives will continue engagement with an independent group in a bid to find a pathway to talks on the ongoing public sector pay dispute. Meetings with a Government-appointed group, chaired by Workplace Relations Commission Chair Kevin Foley, were adjourned last night. On Monday, unions announced plans for a 24-hour strike on Thursday 12 November. Yesterday, Tánaiste Simon Harris said there is "a particularly important window available over the weekend" to resolve the ongoing dispute. Unions have accused the Government of failing to make a credible offer on pay. Talks at the WRC were adjourned last Friday night, with unions saying that a significant impasse had been reached.

stories.title: Bawag received ECB approval for PTSB takeover
stories.summary: Austria's Bawag Group has said it received regulatory approval from the European Central Bank for its takeover of Permanent TSB. The ECB approval means that the potential acquisition has passed a key regulatory hurdle. In a statement, Bawag said it "represents an important milestone toward completion of the transaction". The €1.6 billion deal had been approved by shareholders in July but remains subject by the High Court. However, four shareholders, who are opposing the takeover, called it "derisory". The representatives of the Department of Finance argued that there was no evidence that the State was selling PTSB at a "knock down price".

stories.title: Variety of scores the most pleasing aspect of win v Pumas
stories.summary: With just over 10 minutes played at Aviva Stadium last night, there was a fear that Ireland's sluggish summer form would stretch into the winter. Only a couple of minutes after Mateo Carreras's try sent Argentina 5-0 in front, Dan Sheehan and Craig Casey combined to counter at a ruck and earn a penalty, and from there Ireland never looked back. Andy Farrell remarked after the 42-12 win against Argentina that his side weren't quite "ruthless" enough to kick on in the final quarter and really put their foot on the throat of the Pumas, but the head coach was pleased overall with how his side were clinical when it actually mattered. Their first try had the back three of Mack Hansen, Rob Baloucoune and Hugo Keenan all combining to send the latter in to score, before the second saw Dan Sheehan crash over following a perfectly executed strike from a lineout in the 22. A lineout steal from Ryan Baird gave them their third before half time, and the bonus-point score saw Sam Prendergast (below) pin the ears back and slice through a gap between two backrow forwards. Keenan's hat-trick score saw three forwards – Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and Ryan Baird – string together three delicate passes to send him in under the posts, while the last try saw the forwards go direct and maul their way across the line.

stories.title: Sounding Ireland: how radio became the nation's new confessional
stories.summary: We cannot know what future generations will make of the last half-century's sharing of the profoundly personal on air by people whose public lives are well known to us. It seems that in an increasingly secular society, the media – broadcast and more recently online – has become the country’s new confessional. The appeal of such radio is undeniable. Before the broadcast the presenter advises on the sensitivity of the subject and the circumstances of the recording or live interview. Many listeners cite these interviews as the most memorable and impactful radio experiences of their lives. Perhaps there is some comfort, or some thread of connection formed by hearing that other people’s lives are as complex and fragile as our own. It can also be cathartic for the guest to bare their soul to a nation they have a real relationship with. Sometimes such radio catches the intensity of life on the cusp of dying. When Marian Finucane met Nuala O’Faolain for lunch in 2008, O’Faolain told her friend she was dying. Marian later said that unbelievable though it was, once Nuala told her about her cancer, they started talking about doing an interview. Marian had interviewed Nuala a few times since the publication of her memoir, Are You Somebody? She knew that 'being interviewed live provided [Nuala] with an important means of understanding herself. It was as if answering questions under pressure marshalled all her considerable gifts, allowing her to speak with her wonderful blend of candour, wit and passion.’ And she did. They were recorded within days of the unedited broadcast of the conversation; the stop-starts told their own truth. O’Faolain talked about getting her diagnosis in the emergency department of a New York hospital. She had built her life there and now that life – with her ‘beloved room’, her friends, writing and Ireland – was suddenly reduced to ‘wretchedness, such sourness with life, and fear …’ She wondered ‘how we all get away with our unthinkingness’ and suggested a record ‘that you might play at the end, I know you don’t go playing records, particularly for dying people but still …’ The song was ‘Thíos i Lár an Ghleanna’ (Down in the Middle of the Glen), sung by Albert Fry: ‘Is a Íosa i lár na bhflaithis, tabhair arais an oíche aréir’. Marian Finucane finished the interview by playing the song for O’Faolain. In 2015 Miriam O’Callaghan’s guest on her Sunday morning show was Leo Varadkar. It was his thirty-sixth birthday. She had often interviewed him about policies and crises but said this was ‘not one of those interviews’. During the live interview, he came out as gay to the Irish public – the first serving Irish government minister to do so. The upcoming marriage equality referendum, legislation on surrogacy and whether to change the ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood were coming down the line. As minister for health, Varadkar said he wanted to be honest with people about who he was but also wanted to be ‘an equal citizen in my own country, the country in which I am a member of government and now I am not’. Many parents of gay children called to thank him for speaking out publicly. Others contacted the programme to praise Varadkar for his openness, even if they disagreed with him politically. He hoped that he could be seen as the same person as he was before speaking out. Though Varadkar said he felt better for having done it, he wasn’t sure if the reaction online would be so favourable and hoped the next generation wouldn’t have to come out on air in the same way. In 2025 Brendan O’Connor introduced a recording made earlier in the week of ‘a grown-up conversation that dealt with difficult themes’ with Brenda Fricker, adding playfully that ‘we don’t normally do house calls’. Brendan described the setting for the listener: Brenda in her bed, her beloved dog Juno beside her, surrounded by pictures and possessions of a life fully lived. Their conversation marked the publication of her memoir, She Died Young, and touched on loneliness, happiness and joy, mental health, rape, marriage, miscarriages, suicide and death.
stories.rssSummary: Sounding Ireland is a celebration and a reflection of what listeners heard on RTÉ Radio during its first century: stories told, voices heard and memories made.

stories.summary: "Can I tell you something? Someday soon, we're going for a pint." Screen chemistry: the gold dust that every TV show needs. How many times have you watched something - compelling story, strong cast - and thought, 'Decent, but this would've been so much better with x and y in the roles'? In her TV debut, An Cheathrú Rua-raised writer-creator Eithne Verling has knocked it out of the, well, bay, and front and centre in her story are Star Trek: Voyager's Kate Mulgrew and Love/Hate's John Connors as thrown-together partners Lieutenant Nora Savage and Detective Eddie McDonagh. In a role written specifically for Mulgrew, Nora is a decorated NYPD officer, living out west on an exchange programme with the local force. Connors' character Eddie is a recent arrival from the surveillance unit in Dublin. When the body of a young woman is discovered on a Conamara bog, Nora is pulled in to help the investigation, forming a formidable partnership with Eddie. In person as on screen, Mulgrew and Connors just click - and in a truth-is-stranger-than-fiction twist, the whole series happened because Mulgrew met Verling by chance.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (November 6-8)
stories.summary: From alternative comedy and city-wide events to interactive exhibitions and neighbourhood markets, there's plenty to be doing in Dublin this weekend. Dublin By Night Fest returns to the city on Saturday, 7 November, across Dame St, Parliament St, College Green and Capel St. From 6pm - 10pm, the city centre will transform into a vibrant playground of music, culture, food, fashion and unforgettable experiences. Expect live music, DJs, pop-up performances, immersive experiences, street entertainment, and interactive installations. A new exhibition called Unmasking Nature kicks off in the Digital Hub in the Liberties today, Friday 6 November. Running until 21 November as part of Beta Festival, it's a free, multisensory exhibition exploring the connections between neurodiversity and biodiversity. Unmasking Nature is a sanctuary for restoration. Led by artist AlanJames Burns, this exhibition is open from 12pm - 6pm. Fairview Comedy Club returns after our summer break with our biggest show yet, headlined by none other than Ross McCarney. He will be joined by Sadhbh McLoughlin, Cian Jordan, Matthew Tallon, and MC Neil Downes. The night of laughs will take place at The Strand House in Fairview on Friday, 6 November from 8pm - 10pm. Tickets €17.07. From Thursday, 5 November to Sunday, 8 November 2026, the Contemporary Art Gallery Association (CAGA) and creative producers SoSimpatico will connect the country’s most exciting artists, galleries and cultural institutions to the public. A special series of exhibitions and events that showcase the creative and dynamic energy of Irish contemporary art will be available for curators and the culturally curious. See the full programme here. Neighbourhood Goods is a one-day gathering in Hen's Teeth featuring makers of nice bits & bobs. Expect lovely homewares, food, drinks and some music. Taking place on Saturday, 7 November 2026 from 10am - 5.30pm, the space will welcome Oxmanstown Skincare, SEACHTÓ, Quiet Island, Non Violent Cutlery, Stapleton Tweed, and more.

stories.title: US offers €17m for details on Iran's nuclear programme
stories.summary: The United States is offering a $20 million (€17.9m) reward "and possible relocation" for information about Iran's nuclear programme, the US military said, as President Donald Trump reiterated Tehran wants to make a deal to end the war. Mediators have been working to prevent any resumption of fighting after months of deadlock in the Middle East conflict, which began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Tehran has sought to limit traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption. The offer of a reward comes as Iranian state media reported that Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than it was when the United States and Israel started the war in February. Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said Iran retained control over the strategic waterway and that it would remain closed until its demands were met by the United States. He also said Iran's forces had grown stronger and more confident, state news agency IRNA reported.

stories.title: Still 'opportunity to save jobs' at Poundland - UK PM
stories.summary: The UK Prime Minister has said there is still an "opportunity to save jobs" at Poundland after a meeting between the Government and the chain’s owners this week as the future of the firm and around 11,000 workers hangs in the balance. stories.title: Farrell: 'Some outstanding, really clinical stuff'
stories.summary: A delighted Andy Farrell praised "some really clinical stuff" from his side's attack as they hammered Argentina 42-12 at Aviva Stadium. Three tries in each half, including a Hugo Keenan hat-trick, saw them breeze past an indisciplined Pumas side, as they started their run of home Nations Championship games with a bonus-point win. The 30-point margin perhaps could have been greater, as Ireland took their foot off the pedal in the final 20 minutes when the result had long been decided. And while Farrell admitted his team "missed a chance to be ruthless", he was pleased with how they went about their business when the game was actually in the balance. "Obviously, the scoreline is a good one because not many teams do that to Argentina. They're a very good side and a dangerous side," Farrell said. "We saw that certainly at times, we fought hard to scramble back, so the 12 points [conceded] is very pleasing.

The set list is expected to feature songs from his latest album, Dinner Party, alongside tracks from previous releases, including Heartbreak Weather, The Show: Encore and Flicker.

stories.title: Trump gets ready for a battle on multiple fronts
stories.summary: 1994 was the year of Sony's PlayStation, Pulp Fiction and low-speed Bronco chases. It was also the year of what was called at the time a "Republican revolution". The GOP pulled off stunning victories during the midterm elections under the presidency of Democrat Bill Clinton, winning 230 House seats, 53 Senate seats and 12 gubernatorial races. The significant political shift saw the Democrats lose control of Congress for the first time in decades following widespread public disillusionment with government and it soon led to repeated clashes between the new Republican majority and President Clinton. Thirty-two years later, Democrats have achieved a similarly dramatic and headline inducing reversal of power, with the kind of wins the party has not seen this century. But if 1994 is anything to go by, a resounding midterm win does not necessarily translate into legislative success or future election victory.
stories.rssSummary: History shows a pushback against the party in power during midterm elections, however history also shows that this does not mean the end of a presidency, writes Washington Correspondent Jackie Fox.

stories.summary: There are fears of job losses at laboratory testing service Enfer Medical in Naas, Co Kildare. The Department of Enterprise said it received a collective redundancy notification from the company last month. "The Department received a notification of proposed collective redundancies from Enfer Medical Limited on 6 October 2026," a spokesperson said. "Any further queries should be directed to the company," they added. Enfer Medical said it would not be commenting on a report today from Kildare radio station KFM which said the company is set to cease operations this month. Part of the Enfer Group, Enfer Medical describes itself as a leading clinical laboratory.

There were marquee performances across the board, with Hugo Keenan bagging a hat-trick in his first home game in 21 months. Here's how we rated them after a routine win over a potential World Cup opponent next year. The man of the hour in Dublin, Hugo Keenan's return to a green shirt was a near perfect one. By his own admission, the Leinster star was in the right place at the right time for at least two of his tries, but his second of the night epitomised an outing of sharp attacking rugby from the 2025 test Lion. If not for his full-back's heroics, Ulster's Robert Baloucoune could well have been the main attraction at Lansdowne Road. His work in the build-up to each of Ireland’s first-half tries, including a searing break before Keenan’s opener, showed that the Six Nations 'Rising Star’ from the spring is picking up where he left off. Arguably a quieter night than all other backline options, Robbie Henshaw looked comfortable in deputising for Garry Ringrose in the 13 jersey. The experienced centre defended a threatening Argentinian backline shrewdly, making nine tackles.

stories.summary: The Democrat's success in the US midterm elections saw them take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. It will be the first time US President Donald Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with a Democratic-controlled Congress in both chambers. The blue tsunami, or 'bluenami', sparked political shockwaves and fears of another AI retreat. The US economy has been heavily supported by massive corporate investment in data centres. "The main financial impact is the expectation that there will be a slowdown in AI expansion," said Susannah Streeter, Chief Investment Strategist at Wealth Club. "And because of that and how it underpins the US economy, it's sending ripples around the world," she added.

stories.title: Barry extends scoring streak as Everton see off Coventry
stories.summary: Thierno Barry's hot streak fired Everton into the top five as they came from behind to beat Coventry 3-1. Only Manchester City striker Erling Haaland (nine) has more league goals this season after the 24-year-old’s double turned things around against former Toffees manager Frank Lampard’s side. Barry’s rawness can be a source of frustration, as evidenced in the first half when he wasted a good chance to shoot by failing to get the ball out from under his feet, but he came alive inside the six-yard box after the break. Trailing to Yann Gboho’s first goal for the Sky Blues in only his second league appearance, the Frenchman headed an equaliser before doubling his tally by bundling in a scrappy effort from barely two yards out. Lampard will argue his side should have had at least one penalty when James Tarkowski appeared to pull the hair of Caleb Yirenkyi with the score goalless in the first half, but their own defending left a lot to be desired. Barry has now scored in three successive games for first time for Everton and only second time in his career.

stories.title: Paraguay bank collapse sees president impeached, arrested
stories.summary: Pedro Alliana has become president of Paraguay following the impeachment of his predecessor Santiago Peña over a banking crisis that left almost half the country unable to access their accounts. Senators appointed Mr Alliana, the former vice president, shortly after voting to remove Mr Peña yesterday over the collapse of Uneo Bank, with which he had links. Senate President Basilio Núñez declared Mr Pena "guilty of poor performance in his duties" after 44 out of 45 senators voted in favour of impeachment, with with one voter absent. Hundreds of people waiting outside Congress celebrated his impeachment. "Justice has been done. Now we want him to give us back our money and go to jail," Jessica Aquino, 32, told reporters. Paraguayan authorities placed the former leader under house arrest minutes after his removal, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.

stories.title: Portugal manager Jesus guilt-free over Ronaldo retirement
stories.summary: Portugal boss Jorge Jesus says he feels no guilt over Cristiano Ronaldo's decision to quit international football. The 41-year-old forward announced his Portugal career was over on Thursday after 234 appearances and 146 goals – both of which are records in the men’s game. Ronaldo’s announcement comes less than a month after he was suspended for 30 days and fined €255 by the Portuguese Football Federation after walking out on the national team. The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward had left the camp shortly before a Nations League game against Denmark on 1 October following a row with head coach Jesus. The ban was backdated, so Ronaldo would have been available for upcoming fixtures against Denmark and Wales. Facing the press on Friday to announce his squad for those Nations League games, Jesus – who coached Ronaldo at Saudi club Al Nassr before taking over Portugal in July – said he did not feel responsible for the end of the five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s 23-year international career.

stories.title: Moran cautions against rule changes amid celebrations
stories.summary: Mayo's celebrations of a first All-Ireland title in 75 years are continuing, with the players having spent time with the diaspora in the United States last month. For manager Andy Moran, the emotion of some of the events since July has taken him by surprise, but he says he never doubted that they would get there. Ballaghaderreen clubman Moran played 183 times for the green and red, playing in five All-Ireland finals but never managing to take home a Celtic Cross. This summer, he guided the current generation to the promised land, and he says the players have continued to impress him in the months since. "I'm 43 years of age and it's life changing for me," he said after picking up the 2026 GWA Football Personality of the Year award. "It's a fright, you're literally catching yourself every day.

stories.title: Louth's 1976 Leinster trailblazers honoured
stories.summary: It was a very memorable night for Liz O'Reilly (née Carroll) and her former inter-county colleagues at O’Connell’s GFC in Castlebellingham last Sunday as the Louth ladies football team of 1976 were honoured at a special event. Half a century ago, O’Reilly and her sister Margaret (who now goes under the married name of Cumiskey) were amongst those to feature for the Wee County during their maiden appearance in a Leinster senior football championship final. While Offaly came out on top to claim provincial honours – before also reaching that year’s All-Ireland showpiece at Littleton in Co Tipperary – making it all the way to this stage of the competition was an historic achievement for a Louth side that was still very much in its infancy. Although a number of the panel were introduced to the crowd at half-time in the Louth senior ladies football championship final that took place at the Integral GAA Grounds in Drogheda on 4 October, O’Reilly wasn’t able to make it on the day. However, she was in Castlebellingham six days ago when that trailblazing team from 50 years ago were commemorated and was delighted with how it all unfolded. "It was a very special night to recognise our achievements. 50 years ago we didn’t even think about winning or anything else. We just went out to play, we went out to have a bit of fun.

stories.title: PSNI charge man with murder of missing Limerick woman
stories.summary: Police in Northern Ireland investigating the disappearance and suspected murder of Limerick woman Carrie Mullane in Co Fermanagh have charged a man with her murder. The 35-year-old man is due to appear in court in Dungannon this morning, charged with murder and preventing the lawful burial of a corpse. Ms Mullane (Noonan), 39, has been missing since her arrival in Enniskillen from Limerick on 10 October. The PSNI has been searching for her since officers were made aware of her disappearance on 29 October, but so far have not established her whereabouts. Before announcing the murder charge, police released pictures of a van and boat they believe could be linked to the disappearance. Police believe it is very likely Ms Mullane came to harm shortly after her arrival in Northern Ireland and that establishing the movements of the campervan and boat may provide crucial clues and a clearer picture of what has happened to her.

stories.title: Power skirts with danger but makes cut in Mexico
stories.summary: Séamus Power skirted with danger after a double bogey at the last but managed to sneak inside the cut at the World Wide Technology Championship in Los Cabos in Mexico. Power's late season return to form has seen the Waterford native secure a full PGA Tour card for the 2027 season after his second place finish at the weather-interrupted Butterfield Bermuda Championship less a fortnight ago, and opened with a with a 69. His second round began in superb fashion, with five birdies in his opening seven holes to move to seven-under par. A loose drive at the seventh was the catalyst for his first dropped shot, while finding the greenside bunker at 11 contributed to his second bogey of the round. Power drained a 23ft putt for birdie at the par-4 15th, but endured something of nightmare finish. Greenside after two shots, his chip flew over the opposite side of the green before overshooting his follow-up, eventually settling for seven. It meant a nervy wait for Power to learn his fate as he hovered on the cut line, but five-under par was just enough to seal his place among the top 65 players and ties.

stories.title: Child injured in Waterford arson attack dies in hospital
stories.summary: One of the two children who were critically injured in an arson attack on their home in Waterford city last month, in which four other members of their family were killed, has died in hospital. Six-year-old Elliot English passed away at Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin. His parents, Kim and Philip English, and brothers, 12-year-old Callum and nine-year-old Jayden, also died following the arson attack on their home in the Birchwood estate on 13 October. One more child, who was critically injured in the attack, remains in hospital. The joint funeral mass of Kim, Phillip, Callum and Jayden heard that they were "the salt of the earth and lights in this community" who had done "no wrong to anybody". A total of six people have been arrested to date as part of the garda investigation into the arson attack.

stories.title: Keenan: Ireland moving in the right direction
stories.summary: Hat-trick hero Hugo Keenan believes Ireland are "back in the right direction" after a resounding home 42-12 success over Argentina in round four of the Nations Championship. While Andy Farrell's side fell behind to an early Mateo Carreras try, from the moment Keenan touched down for the first of his three tries on 14 minutes, the hosts never looked in serious danger of a first defeat on Irish soil to the Pumas. It was Ireland’s first outing since a sobering defeat to the All Blacks last July, and coupled with a patchy summer win over Australia, it meant they entered the contest with a number of question marks hanging over the team. Player of the match Keenan was delighted to be back in front of home supporters in Dublin after some injury set-backs and believes the result, and performance, is a stepping stone to better things. "You miss it when you are not there. Some of the lads have gone great when I was injured, it means you have to come back better than ever, be not only consistent, but pushing on as well. "The coaches have challenged us. Johnny (Sexton, assistant coach) has been very good at challenging the backs to do what we have been doing in training, but to present it on the field because we felt in New Zealand, only parts of it we showed what we were capable of.

stories.title: AGSI will not join GRA work-to-rule action next week
stories.summary: The Association of Garda Sergeants and Inspectors (AGSI) has said it will not join a work-to-rule next week which is being planned by the Garda Representative Association (GRA). Members of the GRA are to engage in five days of work-to-rule action coinciding with two major EU Presidency meetings of leaders in Dublin. The association has accused Garda management of being in breach of working-time agreements and of continued over reliance on enforced overtime. Garda management have denied being in breach of agreements and the Garda Commissioner has said that overtime would soon be reduced after forthcoming major events. The AGSI National Executive met today to consider whether to engage in the work-to-rule. "We fully understand the frustration which has led the GRA to announce a work-to-rule," the AGSI said in a statement.

Thomas Markle Snr was taken into custody by FBI agents yesterday. Acting on warrants, FBI agents searched two storage units in LA registered to him, which he had rented since 2008, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

stories.title: A week of cyberattacks and bomb threats: What do we know?
stories.summary: At 8.33am on Friday, an email was sent to publicly listed email addresses at media organisations across Ireland and the UK. Its subject line read: "MESSAGE TO THE WEST". The sender claimed responsibility for bomb threats that had disrupted European flights earlier in the week. Now, the message alleged, an explosive device had been planted in the recipients' buildings. Within the hour, staff were being evacuated from Irish newsrooms and broadcasting schedules were disrupted. An Garda Síochána said it was liaising with the affected media organisations and that the threats would be investigated. It followed a week in which supermarket refrigeration systems were hacked and passenger flights were diverted following bomb threats. The incidents involved different methods. Claims about who was responsible have added to the uncertainty, but their occurrence in the same week does not establish a common source.

stories.title: Man jailed for 20 years over murder of pregnant mother
stories.summary: A man who murdered the pregnant mother of his two children has been jailed for a minimum of 20 years for what the judge described as a "brutal attack on a completely defenceless, heavily pregnant mother" Sarah Montgomery was 32 weeks pregnant when she was murdered by the baby's father, Zak Hughes, in her home in Co Down in June 2025. Hughes, from Ardglen Place in Ardoyne, Belfast, pleaded guilty to her murder and to a charge of child destruction in relation to her unborn baby, whom Ms Mongomery intended to name the baby Liam Arthur. Ms Justice Denise McBride previously imposed a life sentence and today ordered that he serve a tariff of 20 years before he is considered for parole. She sentenced him to 20 years for each charge to run concurrently describing the crime as a "wicked, heinous" act not just against Ms Montgomery, but also her unborn child. The judge said this was "another femicide in a long line of femicides in this jurisdiction", saying Ms Montgomery was not just a statistic and everyone who knew her spoke lovingly about her.

stories.summary: Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic have been investigating threats to air traffic, while a Romanian plane received a bomb threat following a string of hoaxes that have targeted flights and disrupted travel across Europe this week. A flight from Prague to Bucharest operated by Romanian carrier Tarom received a bomb threat. The plane landed at its intended destination, and airport administration officials said the bomb threat proved to be false. In the Danish capital, Copenhagen, police said they were present at the airport for a second consecutive day "in connection with threats directed at air traffic". They said their immediate assessment was that there had been no danger to passengers or to others at the airport. It added that air traffic was proceeding safely and without disruption. Czech police also said they were again dealing with threats against planes today.
